title: Alpha Training
subtitle: Training rhythmic activity commonly associated with relaxed wakefulness
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating alpha training within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain alpha training without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in alpha training.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to alpha training.

sections.explainSimply: Alpha training usually targets activity around 8–12 Hz, often in posterior regions or individualised around peak alpha frequency.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Alpha changes with eyes, arousal, age and task. Training may focus on amplitude, asymmetry or individual peak features, but protocols are not interchangeable.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Evidence is heterogeneous across relaxation, cognition and clinical applications. Demonstrating voluntary modulation does not establish disorder-specific efficacy.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Choosing a camera lens: every method emphasises some information and introduces its own distortions.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand alpha training to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Excess drowsiness or disengagement may look like successful alpha increase.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using alpha training predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Excess drowsiness or disengagement may look like successful alpha increase. Evidence classification: promising for some outcomes; mixed clinical evidence.
